eyebrow: 17.5 mm → 8 mm hollow conical light guide · 100 mm long · mirror wall
author_line: Hengne Li (李衡讷) · South China Normal University · Hengne.Li@cern.ch · Hengne.Li@m.scnu.edu.cn
lead: A specular ray-tracing model of this conical light guide, and a wall shape for which the simulated response map matches the measured 100×100-point scan: the two differ by {rms:.1f}% in the inner aperture, against about 0.8% single-point measurement noise. That wall is not the only one that does so. The scan fixes only a small part of the wall shape.

fact1: RMS difference between measurement and simulation (r < 8 mm, {npts} scan points); point noise is about 0.8%
fact2: The same difference for an ideal cone. An ideal cone responds identically everywhere
fact3: RMS local unevenness needed to reproduce the map. Largest bump {loc_min:.0f} µm, largest dent +{loc_max:.0f} µm

h_wall: A wall that reproduces the scan
p_wall:
Colour is the radial deviation δ of this wall from the ideal CAD cone. It has two parts. The azimuthal mean (panel B) says the whole bore is {mean_lo:.1f}–{mean_hi:.1f} mm narrower than CAD. The local unevenness left after removing that mean (panel A) is what creates the bright and dark structure in the response map, and its RMS is only {loc_rms:.0f} µm.

The response map is very sensitive to some shapes of unevenness. A small deformation at height z on the wall casts a thin arc of light and shade on the entrance face, and the arc moves as z changes, much as in tomography. Unevenness of order 0.03 mm is enough to change the response by a few percent.

How to read this figure: among the walls that reproduce the scan, this is the smoothest one with the least unevenness. It shows how much unevenness is needed at the least. It is not a survey of the real inner surface. The closure test below explains why.
cap_wall: The figure is vector graphics: zoom with the buttons or Ctrl + wheel, drag to pan, and hover over panel A or C to read the deviation at that point.
zoom_hint: Drag to pan, hold Ctrl and scroll to zoom
probe_idle: Hover over panel A or C for a reading
p_maps:
Putting this wall back into the ray tracer, with 40,000 rays per scan point, gives the simulated map in the middle. The off-centre dark spot, the bright ring around it and the bright patches all appear where the measurement has them. The part of the measured structure that departs from the ideal cone correlates with the simulation at {corr:.2f}.

What is left in the inner aperture is mostly point-to-point noise, plus about {excess:.1f}% of structure on a 1 mm scale that the model does not explain (χ²/N = {chi2:.2f}). The outermost 0.4 mm ring of the aperture has larger residuals (about {rms_ring:.0f}% RMS per point). That ring was not fitted; see the limits below.
cap_maps: All three maps use scan-stage coordinates x, y. Bottom left: azimuthally averaged radial profile. Bottom right: the signal once around the ring of radius 4 mm.
step1: Measure the apertureThe edge of the scan is sharp, so the entrance centre, radius and ellipticity (about ±0.03 mm) and the light-spot size (a disc of radius about {spot_r:.2f} mm) are read off directly.
step2: Forward modelWall = CAD cone + a B-spline deviation field (24 azimuthal × 43 axial coefficients). Each source point emits Lambertian rays, they reflect specularly, and the fraction reaching the exit is counted.
step3: Linear responseAround an axisymmetric base wall, azimuthal Fourier modes of the wall are perturbed to get the effect of every coefficient on the map: the Jacobian.
step4: Iterative inversionDamped least squares with a smoothness penalty. After every step the residual is recomputed with a full ray trace, until it stops falling.
p_method:
The inversion rests on a clean property of the ideal cone: for a diffuse point source the transmission equals (Rout/Rin)² = 20.9% everywhere, whatever the source position (conservation of étendue). Any non-uniformity in the measured map must therefore come from the wall departing from the ideal shape.

The fit uses a purpose-written tracer rather than Geant4: one inversion traces of order 1011 rays while the wall shape keeps changing. The tracing kernel runs in OpenCL on this machine's Radeon 8060S at about 50 million rays per second, roughly twenty times faster than 23 CPU cores. Geant4 serves as the independent check.
h_check: How far the result can be trusted
p_check: The checks below answer three different questions: is the tracer right, can the inversion recover a known answer, and how much does the result depend on the assumptions. The first group passes. The closure test shows where the method stops.
row_g4ideal_n: Agrees with the theoretical 0.2090 and with the tracer, and is flat along the radius
row_g4wall_n: The wall was turned into a cavity of 720,000 triangular facets and recomputed with Geant4 optical photons, {npoints} source points × {nphot} photons. Normalised point-by-point scatter {pull_rms:.2f} (1 means pure statistics)
row_gpu_n: In double precision at most one ray differs per point; single precision is unbiased (mean difference 2×10<sup>−7</sup>)
row_recip_n: The flux from entrance to exit must equal the flux the other way. A wrong intersection or surface normal breaks this identity
row_closure_n: Known wall (7 bumps and dents) → noisy synthetic scan → same pipeline. The synthetic scan is fitted down to the noise, so the pipeline itself converges properly
row_closure2_n: Fails. The recovered wall is almost uncorrelated with the true one: true local unevenness {rms_true:.0f} µm, recovered {rms_rec:.0f} µm. Only inside the subspace the scan can see (about 100 shape combinations) does the correlation reach {corr_vis}, and the true wall has just {frac_vis:.0f}% of its deformation there
row_refl_n: With the mirror reflectivity as a free parameter the fit gives 0.94, but it still needs geometric deformation of the same size and does not fit clearly better, so the result is quoted for a perfect mirror
cap_closure: Closure test. Left: the true local unevenness put in. Middle: what the inversion recovers from the synthetic scan (same colour scale). Right: azimuthal mean profile. The two walls give the same response map within the noise.
cav1: The solution is not uniqueDifferent walls give the same response map. The scan constrains about 100–150 combinations of the wall shape (down to 1–10 µm); a broad, gentle bump leaves almost no trace even at 0.2–0.3 mm height. Shown here is the wall with the least unevenness among those that fit.
cav2: The azimuthal mean profile is poorly fixedIt is strongly degenerate with the overall signal scale and the exit radius, and different fits return different profiles. Only the entrance radius (measured directly) and the statement that the bore is narrower than CAD are reliable. Two independent fits in this work returned profiles about 0.5 mm apart, with local unevenness of 13 µm and 44 µm RMS, and both reproduce the scan.
cav3: Everything is blamed on geometryBy assumption the mirror reflectivity is 1, the PMT is uniform and the source is an ideal Lambertian. Real reflectivity variations, the seam of the reflective film or photocathode non-uniformity would all be read as wall unevenness.
cav4: The entrance rimIn the outermost 0.4 mm ring the azimuthally averaged residual is still 2–4%. The measurement drops earlier than the model inside the aperture but shows no tail outside, as if a band about 0.1 mm wide at the rim were lossy (a chamfer, or film that stops short of the edge). This is below the model resolution and was not fitted.
cav5: What would pin down the real wallIndependent information: scans with a collimated beam at several incidence angles, angle-resolved readout at the exit, a scan from the exit side, or direct profilometry of the wall. Each new measurement constrains a further set of shape combinations.
cav6: Orientation of the azimuthφ is defined by the scan x and y. Relating it to the hardware needs the orientation of the stage axes with respect to the light guide, and which of the 4 cells was scanned.
p_files: The code is a stand-alone toolkit, LGWallRecon: the tracer (CPU and GPU), the inversion pipeline, the closure test, the Geant4 check and user manuals in Chinese and English.

f2_foot: Inner aperture (r < 8 mm): RMS residual {rms:.2f}%; point noise about 0.8%. An ideal cone gives a flat response and cannot explain the measured structure.
f3_title: Closure test: how well is a known wall recovered?
f3_sub: Seven bumps and dents on a known wall, a noisy synthetic scan traced from it, then the same inversion pipeline. Both maps share one colour scale.
f3_foot: Both walls give the same response map within the noise (residual {map_rms:.2f}%), yet the walls correlate at only {corr_all:.2f}: true unevenness {rms_true:.0f} µm, recovered {rms_rec:.0f} µm. The scan does not determine the wall uniquely.
